11.1.crux: A force is a push or a pull on an object.

cards.title: Push or pull?
say: Every time we move something, we push it or pull it.
A push or a pull on an object is called a force.

cards.title: Forces all day
say: Look around: you'll find pushes and pulls everywhere.
cards.think: Is lifting a bucket a push or a pull?

cards.title: What a force can do

items.name: Change direction
items.eg: Hit a ball with a bat

say: We will explore each of these effects in the next topics.

crux_points: A force is a push or a pull.
Forces act all around us in daily life.
A force can start, stop, speed up, turn or reshape objects.

quiz.q: Opening a drawer is an example of…
quiz.why: You pull the drawer towards you.

quiz.q: A force is…
quiz.why: Any push or pull on an object is a force.

11.2.crux: A force always comes from an interaction between at least two objects.

cards.title: It takes two
say: A car standing alone won't move by itself.
When you push it, you and the car interact: that's when a force acts.

cards.title: Interactions everywhere

items.sub: Pull a rope in opposite directions

say: At least two objects must interact for a force to come into play.

cards.title: Both feel it

steps.text: You push a wall
The wall pushes back on your hands
You can feel the push on your palms

say: In an interaction, both objects feel a force.

crux_points: A force needs at least two interacting objects.
Examples: a person pushing a car, two teams in tug of war.
Both objects in an interaction feel a force.

quiz.q: How many objects are needed for a force to act?
quiz.why: A force arises from an interaction between at least two objects.

quiz.q: A ball lying alone on the floor…
options: Won't move unless something interacts with it
quiz.why: Without an interaction, there is no force to move it.

11.3.crux: A force has a size (magnitude) and a direction; forces in the same direction add up, and forces in opposite directions work against each other.

cards.title: Same direction: forces add
say: Two friends pushing a heavy box the same way move it more easily.

cards.title: Opposite directions: forces fight

cols.head: Unequal pulls
cells: Rope moves towards the stronger team

say: In a tug of war, forces act in opposite directions.
The overall force left over is called the net force.
cards.remember: Same direction: add. Opposite directions: subtract.

cards.title: Size and direction
say: To describe a force fully, we need both its strength (magnitude) and its direction.
If either changes, the effect changes.

crux_points: Forces have magnitude (size) and direction.
Forces in the same direction add up.
Opposite forces subtract; equal opposite forces cancel out.

quiz.q: Two teams pull a rope equally hard in opposite directions. What happens?
quiz.why: Equal and opposite forces cancel, so the net force is zero.

quiz.q: Why is it easier for two people to push a box together in the same direction?
quiz.why: Forces in the same direction add to a bigger net force.

11.4.crux: A force can change an object's state of motion: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down or change its direction.

cards.title: State of motion

cols.head: In motion
cells: Has a speed and a direction

say: The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and its direction.
Being at rest means having zero speed.

cards.title: Changes a force can make

steps.text: Kick a ball at rest: it starts moving
Kick it again in the same direction: it speeds up
Goalkeeper catches it: it stops
A player heads it sideways: its direction changes

say: One game of football shows every kind of change in motion.
cards.remember: A force can change speed, direction, or both.

cards.title: A force doesn't always move things
say: A force may be too small to move a heavy object.
But it still acts on it.

crux_points: State of motion = speed and direction (rest means zero speed).
A force can start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn a moving object.
A force does not always cause motion.

quiz.q: A batsman hits a ball and it changes direction. This shows a force can…
quiz.why: The bat's force changes the ball's direction (and speed).

quiz.q: An object at rest has a speed of…
quiz.why: Being at rest means not moving: zero speed.

11.5.crux: A force can change the shape of an object, like squeezing a balloon, stretching a rubber band or rolling out dough.

cards.title: Shapes change
say: When you press, squeeze or stretch something, you change its shape.

cards.title: Back or not?
say: Some objects return to their shape when the force is removed. Others stay changed.

cards.title: All the effects of force
say: A force can do one or more of these things at the same time.
cards.remember: Force can change motion AND shape.

crux_points: A force can change the shape of an object.
Some objects spring back; others stay changed.
Force affects speed, direction and shape.

quiz.q: Rolling out dough to make a chapati shows that force can…
quiz.why: Pressing the dough changes its shape.

quiz.q: Which object returns to its shape after you stop pressing?
quiz.why: A sponge springs back; clay and dough stay changed.

11.6.crux: Contact forces act only when objects touch: muscular force from our muscles, and friction, which slows moving things down.

cards.title: Muscular force
say: The force from the action of muscles is called muscular force.
We use it to walk, lift, run and even to breathe and digest food.

cards.title: Friction

steps.text: A ball rolls along the ground
It slowly slows down
It stops: friction from the ground acted against its motion

say: Friction acts between two surfaces in contact and opposes motion.
A ball rolling on a rough field stops sooner than on a smooth floor.

cards.title: Contact needed
say: Next topic: forces that act without touching.

crux_points: Contact forces act when objects touch each other.
Muscular force comes from muscles.
Friction acts between surfaces and opposes motion.

quiz.q: A rolling ball slowly stops because of…
quiz.why: Friction between the ball and the ground opposes its motion.

quiz.q: Which is a contact force?
quiz.why: Muscular force works only when you touch the object.

11.7.crux: Non-contact forces act from a distance: magnetic force, electrostatic force and the gravitational force of the Earth (gravity).

cards.title: Three non-contact forces

items.name: Magnetic
items.eg: A magnet attracts iron, or repels another magnet's like pole

items.name: Electrostatic
items.eg: A rubbed comb or straw attracts bits of paper

items.name: Gravitational
items.eg: The Earth pulls everything towards it

say: These forces act even when the objects don't touch.

cards.title: Gravity

items.text: A ball thrown up comes down

say: The Earth pulls every object towards itself. This pull is called gravity.
In fact, every object in the universe attracts every other object.
cards.remember: Gravity is an attractive force: it always pulls.

cards.title: Charged objects

steps.text: Rub a plastic straw or comb with paper or hair
It becomes charged
Bring it near small bits of paper: they jump towards it

say: The force from a charged object is called electrostatic force.

crux_points: Non-contact forces act from a distance.
Magnetic and electrostatic forces can attract or repel.
Gravity is the Earth's pull on everything; every object attracts every other.

quiz.q: A mango falls from a tree because of…
quiz.why: The Earth's gravitational pull brings it down.

quiz.q: A comb rubbed on hair attracts bits of paper. This is…
quiz.why: The rubbed comb gets charged; charged objects exert electrostatic force.

11.8.crux: Pressure is force acting on a unit area; the same force pressing on a smaller area gives a bigger pressure.

cards.title: Same push, different effect
say: Push a pointed nail and a flat block with the same force.
The nail sinks in, because its force is concentrated on a small area.

cards.title: The pressure rule
say: Pressure = force ÷ area on which it acts.
Smaller area → bigger pressure. Bigger area → smaller pressure.

cards.title: Pressure in daily life

cols.head: Large area: less pressure
cells: Porter's round cloth on the head

say: A sharp knife cuts easily because its thin edge has a tiny area.
Wide straps spread the bag's weight, so it presses less on your shoulders.

crux_points: Pressure = force ÷ area.
The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure.
Sharp tools have small areas; wide straps spread force over large areas.

quiz.q: Why do school bags have wide straps?
options: They spread the force over a large area, so less pressure
quiz.why: A larger area means less pressure on the shoulders.

quiz.q: Which part is marked '?'
options: The pointed tip: small area, high pressure
quiz.why: The nail's point has a tiny area, so the pressure there is large.

11.9.crux: Liquids and gases press on the walls of their containers; liquid pressure increases with depth.

cards.title: Deeper means more pressure
say: Make holes at different heights in a bottle full of water.
Water from the lowest hole shoots out farthest: pressure is greatest at the bottom.

cards.title: Pushing on the walls

steps.text: Make holes all around a bottle at the same height
Fill it with water
Water comes out of every hole equally far

say: Liquids press on the walls of the container in all directions.
At the same depth, the pressure is the same.

cards.title: Gases press too

items.sub: Air inside pushes the walls out

say: Gases also exert pressure on the walls of their containers.

cards.title: Why dams are wide at the bottom

items.name: Top of dam
items.note: Little water pressure: wall can be thin

items.name: Bottom of dam
items.note: Greatest pressure: wall must be thickest

say: Because pressure increases with depth, dams are built much thicker at the bottom.

crux_points: Liquids and gases exert pressure on the walls of their containers.
Liquid pressure increases with depth.
At the same depth, liquid pressure is the same in all directions.

quiz.q: Which hole's jet is marked '?'
options: The bottom hole's jet: the farthest
quiz.why: Pressure is greatest at the bottom, so that jet shoots farthest.

quiz.q: Why is a dam thicker at the bottom?
options: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom
quiz.why: Liquid pressure increases with depth.

11.10.crux: The air around us presses on everything; this atmospheric pressure is very large, but we don't feel crushed because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.

cards.title: Air has pressure

items.name: Atmosphere
items.note: A blanket of air many kilometres high

say: The pressure exerted by the air around us is called atmospheric pressure.

cards.title: The rubber sucker

steps.text: Press a rubber sucker on a smooth surface
Most of the air between them is pushed out
Air pressure outside holds the sucker firmly in place

say: It's hard to pull the sucker off because atmospheric pressure presses on it from outside.
cards.remember: The air outside pushes; there's little air inside to push back.

cards.title: Why aren't we crushed?

cols.head: Inside
cells: Pressure inside our body is equal

say: The air on a 15 cm × 15 cm area presses with a force as large as the pull of gravity on 225 kg!
We're not crushed because the pressure inside our bodies is equal to it.

cards.title: A famous experiment

steps.text: Otto von Guericke joined two metal hemispheres
He pumped out the air from inside
Eight horses on each side couldn't pull them apart

say: Atmospheric pressure pushed the halves together so strongly.

crux_points: Air exerts pressure: atmospheric pressure.
It holds a rubber sucker to a wall.
We aren't crushed because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.

quiz.q: What holds a rubber sucker against the wall?
quiz.why: Air pressure outside presses it on; there is little air inside to push back.

quiz.q: Why don't we feel crushed by atmospheric pressure?
options: The pressure inside our body balances it
quiz.why: Our body's internal pressure equals the atmospheric pressure.
